title: Exodus 7–13
notes: Study aids companion for OT reading

footnotes.text: When the Savior was crucified, the Roman soldiers went to break His legs to induce death. However, they refrained when they saw that He had already died (seeJohn 19:31–33). John taught, “These things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled, A bone of him shall not be broken” (John 19:36).

Gerrit W. Gong, “Hosanna and Hallelujah—The Living Jesus Christ: The Heart of Restoration and Easter,”EnsignorLiahona, May 2020, 54. The blood on the entrances of the Israelite homes was also a sign to the Lord of their obedience and trust in Him and His prophet. In our day, the Lord used the imagery of the destroying angel passing by when He described the blessings of obeying the Word of Wisdom (seeDoctrine and Covenants 89:18–21).
See Berlin and Brettler,The Jewish Study Bible, 118, note onExodus 12:14–20.

After the Israelites escaped Egypt, the Lord instituted the annual feast of unleavened bread as a continuing memorial of their deliverance. This feast lasted for seven days. The first and seventh days were Sabbaths and days of holy convocation (seeExodus 12:15–17; Bible Dictionary, “Feasts”).
See Berlin and Brettler,The Jewish Study Bible, 117, note onExodus 12:8; see alsoExodus 1:14.
SeeExodus 13:2, 12. Originally, the firstborn male from each family was to serve in a priestly role in the tabernacle. Later, the tribe of Levi exclusively filled that role (seeNumbers 3:12).
Boyd K. Packer, “Atonement, Agency, Accountability,”Ensign, May 1988, 72.

“[Some] interpreters suggest a symbolic correlation between each plague and an Egyptian deity, assuming they were each meant to demonstrate Jehovah’s superiority over a specific god. This explanation is difficult to confirm in every case. … [However,] there is no doubt that the plagues as a whole were intended to demonstrate the power of Jehovah over the Egyptian pantheon, which included the divine Pharaoh himself” (Richard Neitzel Holzapfel and others,Jehovah and the World of the Old Testament: An Illustrated Reference for Latter-day Saints[2009], 90). See also Kerry Muhlestein, “‘What I Will Do to Pharaoh’: The Plagues Viewed as a Divine Confrontation with Pharaoh,” inFrom Creation to Sinai: The Old Testament through the Lens of the Restoration, ed. Daniel L. Belnap and Aaron P. Schade (2021), 450.
The phrase “glory over me” in the King James Version can also be phrased “I grant you preeminence to declare” (seeExodus 8:9, footnotea).

“Allowing Pharaoh to specify the time for removing the frogs should reinforce the lesson of the Lord’s unique power: He can end a plague at the very moment specified” (Adele Berlin and Marc Zvi Brettler, eds.,The Jewish Study Bible, 2nd ed.[2014], 111, note onExodus 8:6).
